title: Children in foster care give the most positive answers in Ofsted's 2026 survey
standfirst: Ofsted's annual questionnaire of children in care and residential settings found those living with foster carers were the most likely to say they feel safe, are listened to and had done something fun in the past week.
body: Ofsted has published the results of its 2026 children's social care questionnaires, the yearly online survey it sends to children and adults connected with children's homes, fostering and adoption services, supported accommodation, residential family centres, boarding schools, residential special schools and further education colleges with residential provision in England. The survey ran for seven weeks, from 2 February to 22 March 2026, and the report was published on 29 October.

Ofsted received 46,900 responses across all the groups it surveyed, of which 8,360 came from children, down from 8,880 in 2025. Across every setting, 96% of children said they feel safe where they live or stay, 91% said they feel listened to always or most of the time, and 77% said they spend time with people who are important to them.

Children living with foster carers stood out. Ofsted says they reported overwhelmingly positive experiences across all of its questions, and they were the group most likely to say they feel safe always, at 92%. Some 98% said the people looking after them listen to them always or most of the time, and 95% gave positive answers when asked whether they are asked about things that matter to them, the highest of any setting alongside supported accommodation.

Children in foster care were also the most likely to say they get on with the other children in the household, at 92%, up from 88% in 2025 and close to the 91% recorded in 2024. And 96% said they had done something fun in the previous week, the highest rate of any setting and unchanged for three years. The one area with more room to improve was time with important people: in Ofsted's tables, 53% of children in foster care said they always spend time with people who matter to them and 28% said most of the time.

Ofsted uses the answers, together with earlier inspection findings and other information, to decide when to inspect a service and what to focus on. Trained staff read responses as they arrive and pass any safeguarding concern straight to inspectors. The report notes that not every child in a fostering setting is looked after, as some are receiving short breaks. Answers from adults, including foster carers and kinship carers, are published separately as data rather than in the report.

For anyone thinking about fostering, the survey is a reminder of what carers are already giving children day to day: a safe home, someone who listens, and ordinary family life. Around two in three looked-after children in England live with foster carers, according to the report, and the government has set a goal of creating 10,000 more foster places over this Parliament. Ofsted runs the survey every year, so current carers whose fostering service is asked to take part can encourage the children they look after to have their say.

title: UK foster carer pay by council 2026-27: what 25 councils publish
standfirst: Weekly allowances in the 25 councils we have checked run from £176 for a baby to £337.40 for a teenager, and the fees paid to carers on top vary even more.
body: Fostering Today has now published the 2026-27 foster carer allowances for 25 UK councils, each taken from the council's own website, committee papers or rate schedules and linked to that source on our council pages. Twenty of the councils are in England and five in Scotland. This summary brings those pages together so prospective carers, current carers and anyone writing about fostering can compare what councils say they pay. We will update it as more councils are added.

The weekly allowance is the money paid for each child's day-to-day costs, and it rises with age. Across the 23 councils that publish it as a separate figure, the lowest rate for the youngest age band is £176 a week, paid by Calderdale and Northumberland for children up to two, and the highest is £210 a week, paid by Kent for children under two. For the oldest children, seven councils (Calderdale, Leicester, Newcastle, Northumberland, Rochdale, Wakefield and Walsall) pay £267 a week and Staffordshire pays £267.50, while Coventry pays £337.40 and Lincolnshire £331.66 for young people aged 16 and over. The gap between £267 and £337.40 is £70.40 a week for a teenager in the same age band, or £3,660.80 over a year.

Two councils publish a single weekly total that combines the child's allowance with the carer's reward or professional fee instead of listing them separately. Bracknell Forest's Tier 1 totals run from £304.83 to £480.34 a week depending on the child's age, and Thurrock's from £415 to £516 at its standard Care Skills rate and up to £568 at Care Skills+.

In Scotland, East Ayrshire, Highland, Scottish Borders and Shetland all publish the same three allowance rates, £177.68, £206.71 and £283.35 a week, which Shetland's page notes match the Scottish Recommended Allowance for the year. Aberdeenshire pays more in every age band, from £191.13 to £307.79 a week.

Fees are where councils differ most. Nineteen of the 25 publish a weekly fee, skills or reward payment for mainstream carers on top of the allowance; two publish combined totals; Aberdeenshire pays an annual skills payment starting at £10,431.21 for newly approved carers; Highland's schedule shows fees only for specialist and intensive carers; and the pages for Lincolnshire and Shetland list no fee. Starting levels vary widely: Leicester's Level 1 payment for newly approved carers is £50 a week per child, Wakefield's Skill Level 1 is £53 and Central Bedfordshire's first tier is £100, while Croydon's entry-level skills fee is £325 a week. Several councils, including Bristol and Staffordshire, pay no fee at their first level.

Each council's page on Fostering Today shows its full age bands, fee levels and extras such as birthday, holiday and festival payments, with the date we checked it. Age bands and fee structures are not the same from one council to the next, so the fairest comparison is the full table for the area you live in, and the fostering team can confirm what would apply to you. Our pay calculator puts council and agency figures side by side.

title: Welsh councils must send first care sufficiency plans by 1 December as new rules take effect
standfirst: Regulations requiring every Welsh council to publish an annual plan for finding enough local homes for children in care, including foster homes, came into force on 26 October 2026.
body: New regulations requiring local authorities in Wales to prepare annual sufficiency plans for the children they look after came into force on 26 October 2026. On the same day the Welsh Government published guidance and a template for councils to use, setting out what the plans must cover and how they will be approved, submitted and revised.

According to the Welsh Government's November newsletter on removing profit from children's care, each plan will assess the current and future care and accommodation needs of the children a council looks after and explain how it will secure enough suitable places for them. The regulations list the information every plan has to contain. Councils must send their first drafts to Welsh Ministers by 1 December 2026 and publish them, once approved, by 31 March 2027.

The plans are part of Wales's wider move, under the Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025, to a not-for-profit model for children's homes, fostering and secure accommodation. The newsletter repeats that from 1 April 2027 existing for-profit providers will not be able to approve new foster carers or add beds unless they have re-established as a not-for-profit body, and says Care Inspectorate Wales is updating its FAQs and contacting independent fostering services directly. The Welsh Government expects to publish its response to the consultation on limiting further for-profit growth this month.

The newsletter also reports two developments aimed at carers. Foster Wales, through which all 22 Welsh councils work together, launched a new Learning and Development Framework in September 2026, with new modules, a digital e-book and an online portal, and showcased it at its annual conference in Llangollen on 23 September. Separately, ADSS Cymru, the body representing social services directors, has worked with Foster Wales on a national fostering cost model, a framework for understanding the costs of recruiting, approving and supporting foster carers.

What this means for you: sufficiency plans are where councils set out how many and what kind of placements they expect to need, so the published plans should show where demand for local foster carers is greatest, for example for teenagers or sibling groups. If you are thinking about fostering in Wales, your council's fostering team, working as part of Foster Wales, remains the main route in alongside not-for-profit agencies. Foster Wales says its councils are working together to help foster carers who want to transfer from for-profit agencies.

What happens next: draft plans go to Welsh Ministers by 1 December, the consultation response on the 2027 restrictions is due in November, and approved plans must be published by the end of March 2027. ADSS Cymru is holding an online briefing on the changes on 12 January 2027. We will report the consultation outcome when it is published.
